Iran is heading into winter facing a worsening natural gas shortage, as damage to key processing facilities during the war with the United States and Israel compounds years of chronic supply deficits.

President Masud Pezeshkian warned on November 21 that the country would likely face energy supply problems this winter.

"Even before this, we were facing an energy imbalance, and now attacks on the country's gas infrastructure have made this imbalance worse. We expect to face problems in the winter," Pezeshkian said.

He said the attacks had knocked out 240 million cubic meters of daily gas production capacity, of which about 100 million cubic meters had since been restored. That leaves around 140 million cubic meters a day offline, on top of a prewar shortfall that Pezeshkian put at 250 million to 300 million cubic meters a day during peak consumption.

Officials' estimates of this winter's shortage range from 400 million to 530 million cubic meters per day. National Iranian Gas Company chief Saeed Tavakoli has warned that at least 11 provinces could face supply difficulties, while government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani has cautioned that cuts could reach Tehran if consumption stays high.

The shortages threaten further disruption to industry. Iran has already restricted gas supplies to some factories, and there have been reports of production disruptions in the cement and petrochemical sectors.

Meanwhile, Deputy Energy Minister Mostafa Rajabi Mashhadi has warned that fueling power plants will be harder this winter because of reduced gas output, and the government expects to keep burning mazut, a heavy fuel oil, to make up the shortfall.

State electricity company Tavanir began rolling blackouts for homes and businesses on November 22. Its chief executive, Mohammad Allahdad, blamed the move on fuel shortages at power plants.

Iran has the world's second-largest proven natural gas reserves but has struggled for years to supply its own population. International sanctions have scared off foreign investment and technology, while aging fields, a decaying pipeline network, and heavily subsidized, wasteful consumption have left output trailing demand every winter.
